title: Lists & Keys
summary: **Lists & keys** is how React renders collections: you turn an array into elements with `.map`, and give each element a stable, unique `key` so React can track items correctly across re-renders.

subtopics.title: Mapping arrays to elements
subtopics.explanation: `.map()` makes a new value for every item in an array. In React, it often turns each item into a component or element. Think of a bakery turning each order on a list into one prepared box.

subtopics.title: The key prop
subtopics.explanation: A key is a stable label React uses to recognize one item in a list. Use an item's id when possible. React uses keys like name tags to match people as they move around.

subtopics.title: Stable vs index keys
subtopics.explanation: A stable key belongs to the item, such as its database id. An index only tells its current position. If items move, position labels can point to the wrong person, like numbered seats after everyone swaps.
subtopics.example: items.map((item, i) => <Row key={item.id} />) // stable, not key={i}

subtopics.title: Key uniqueness
subtopics.explanation: Keys need to be unique only among items in the same list. Two different lists may reuse the same values. Think of table numbers: each table needs a distinct number in its own room.

subtopics.title: Fragments in lists
subtopics.explanation: A Fragment groups multiple elements without adding a wrapper to the page. In a list, use `React.Fragment` when the group needs a key. It is like carrying two related items together without another box.

subtopics.title: Reconciliation
subtopics.explanation: Reconciliation is React's comparison of the previous and next page descriptions. Keys help it match list items correctly. It is like comparing two class photos by name instead of guessing from seat position.

subtopics.title: Generating ids for keyless data
subtopics.explanation: If an item has no id, create one when the item is first made and save it with the data. Do not create a new id during every render. It is like assigning a permanent library card, not a new one each visit.

foundations.overview: A list in React starts with an array of data. Use `.map()` to turn each item into a page element. Give each element a stable key, so React can recognize it when the list changes. Keys are like name tags at a busy event.
foundations.formalDefinition: Rendering a list means returning an array of React elements, typically via `items.map(item => <Item key={item.id} ... />)`. The `key` is a special prop (not passed to your component) that React uses during reconciliation to identify which items are the same across renders.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every UI shows lists — feeds, tables, menus, search results. Doing it correctly (and choosing good keys) is essential, and the index-as-key bug is one of the most common sources of subtle, hard-to-find state corruption in React apps.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of keys as name tags React puts on each item. When the list changes, React reads the name tags to figure out which items stayed, which left, and which are new — then it reuses the matching DOM and component state instead of rebuilding everything.
foundations.browserPerspective: During reconciliation, React compares the new list of elements to the previous one by key. Matching keys mean 'same element' — React reuses that DOM node and its component state, updating only changed attributes. Missing or unstable keys force React to guess by position, which can move state to the wrong item.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Rendering search results, to-do items, chat messages, table rows, dropdown options, tabs, and any data that arrives as an array from an API.
foundations.businessImpact: List bugs show up as inputs that keep the wrong text after a row is deleted, checkboxes that 'jump' to other rows, and flickering — all of which look broken to users and erode trust in the product.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Choosing stable keys prevents an entire class of state-association bugs and unnecessary DOM work. The index-as-key mistake is so common it is a standard code-review and interview check.
foundations.performanceImpact: Good keys let React reuse DOM nodes and skip rebuilding unchanged items, which keeps long lists fast. Bad keys force React to recreate or mismatch nodes, causing extra DOM work and visible flicker.
commonUseCases: Rendering API results (users, products, posts) as rows or cards
To-do and shopping lists where items are added, removed, and reordered
Tables with selectable or editable rows
Dropdowns, tab strips, and navigation menus

commonMisconceptions.myth: Using the array index as the key is fine.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is only safe when the list is static (never reordered, inserted into, or filtered). When items move, index keys make React associate state with the wrong item.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The `key` prop is available inside the child component as props.key.
commonMisconceptions.reality: `key` is consumed by React and is never passed to your component. If you need the value inside the child, pass it again under a different prop name.

visualExplorer.title: How React matches list items by key
visualExplorer.caption: See how React uses keys to decide which items to keep, move, add, or remove when a list changes.

config.intro: When a list re-renders, React compares the new elements to the old ones by their key to figure out what actually changed.

steps.name: Map data to elements
steps.detail: items.map(item => <Item key={item.id} .../>) turns each data object into a keyed element.

steps.name: React reads the keys
steps.detail: On re-render, React pairs up old and new elements that share the same key — those are 'the same item'.

steps.name: Reuse matched items
steps.detail: For matching keys, React reuses the existing DOM node and component state, updating only changed props.

steps.name: Insert and remove
steps.detail: Keys present only in the new list are mounted; keys only in the old list are unmounted — exactly the items that changed.

steps.name: Index keys go wrong on reorder
steps.detail: If keys are array indexes, reordering keeps the same indexes, so React thinks nothing moved and leaves state attached to the wrong item.

interactiveExamples.title: Map an array to a list
interactiveExamples.explanation: Use .map to turn each data item into an element, and give each a stable key from the data (here, the unique id).
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A bulleted list of the three user names, each backed by a stable id key.

interactiveExamples.title: Fragments as list items
interactiveExamples.explanation: When each item needs to render multiple sibling nodes without an extra wrapper, use the explicit Fragment form and put the key on the Fragment.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A definition list where each item renders a <dt> and <dd> pair, keyed on the Fragment, with no extra wrapper element.

keyTakeaways: Render lists by mapping a data array to elements: `items.map(item => <Item key={item.id} ... />)`.
Every list item needs a key that is unique among its siblings; React uses it during reconciliation.
Key by a stable id, not the array index — index keys corrupt per-item state on reorder, insert, or delete.
Never use Math.random() as a key; it changes every render and re-creates every item.
The key prop is consumed by React and is not passed to your component — re-pass it as another prop if needed.
